newsitem.title: INDIA: India must speed up oil sector reforms - Kleinwort.
newsitem.headline: India must speed up oil sector reforms - Kleinwort.

text.p: The deregulation of India's state-controlled oil and gas industry must be completed faster than the four-to-six years recommended by a government panel, securities firm Kleinwort Benson Securities Ltd said on Monday.

"We believe that the deregulation process should take a maximum of three years as opposed to the 'R' Group's three-stage four to six years proposal," the London-based securities house said in a report.
It said a longer transition period will allow vested interests more time to undermine reforms.

"Time is working against the country. The longer it takes to complete energy reform, the more India will become hostage to outside events which would have severe implications for the domestic economy," the report warned.

Kleinwort said the recent 'R' group report -- a government panel set up to make recommendations on oil sector reforms -- takes the scenario of strongly rising oil and gas demand virtually for granted.
"The crucial issues of conservation and substitution have been virtually ignored," it said.
Kleinwort faulted India's energy reforms for focusing only on oil and gas and neglecting coal and hydro, two of the country's largest sources of energy.
It said the essence of any energy reform process should be to play on a country's strengths rather than compound its weaknesses.

"Contrary to conventional wisdom, India is not poor in energy resources - it only poor in reserves of oil and gas," it said. It quoted latest estimates saying only 18 percent of the nation's hydro resources and a mere one percent of the coal reserves are being exploited.

"In the case of hydro power alone, the resources of the (northern state of) Himachal Pradesh state are almost certainly equivalent to another Bombay High type of discovery if not much more." The Bombay High offshore field supplies the bulk of India's oil and gas production.

The report called for creation of an energy body to co-ordinate overall energy strategy, reporting directly to the Cabinet. It said state-run Coal India Ltd should be restructured and potential coal reserves outside its control should be opened up aggressively to private investment.
It said latest clean coal technology should be used to encourage use of coal in power generation.
"The customs duty on imported coal should be ended to reduce the attractions of importing oil and use international competition as a spur for domestic reforms ," it said.
The securities firm said there was a strong case for conservation and energy substitution.

"It has been variously estimated that long-term savings of 15-30 percent, equivalent to as much as one million barrels a day (mbd/d) of oil imports by the end of the ninth plan (2002), could be achieved if a serious conservation and substitution policy were adopted," it said.
"Every 10 percent rise in demand is equivalent to a 150,000 b/d increase in crude oil imports," the report said.
